Michelle Obama
[1] In a special personal essay, excerpted here, in honor of Mother’s Day,
Michelle Obama shares memories of her mom, Marian Robinson, and women
who shaped the extraordinary life of an ordinary girl from Chicago who would
grow up to be the wife of the President of the United States.
[2] My mother is a woman who chooses her words carefully. She’ll sometimes
speak in clipped sentences, her wisdom packed into short bursts and punctuated
with an infectious smile or a wry laugh. It’s a style that makes her a favorite of
everyone she meets – a sweet, witty companion who doesn’t need the limelight.
[3] As I’ve grown older, I’ve seen how her manner in conversation also reflects
her approach to parenting. Because when it came to raising her kids, my mom
knew that her voice was less important than allowing me to use my own.

[4] That meant she listened a lot more than she lectured. Growing up, she was
willing to endure endless questioning from me – Why did we have to eat eggs
for breakfast? Why do people need jobs? Why are the houses bigger in other
neighborhoods? She didn’t chide me if I scrapped with some of the neighbor
kids or challenged my ornery grandfather when I thought he was being a little
too ornery. She listened intently to the lunchtime conversations I had with my
schoolmates over bologna sandwiches, and nodded patiently along to tales of my
contentious piano lessons with my great-aunt Robbie.
[5] In today’s world, it’s easy to hear all that and think that Marian Robinson
was bordering on negligent, that she was letting the kids rule the roost. But the
reality was far from that. She and my father, Fraser, were wholly invested in
their children, pouring a deep and durable foundation of goodness and honesty,
of right and wrong, into my brother and me. After that, they simply let us be
ourselves.
[6] I see now how important that kind of freedom is for all children,
particularly for girls with flames of their own – flames the world might try to
dim. It’s up to us, as mothers and mother-figures, to give the girls in our lives
the kind of support that keeps their flame lit and lifts up their voices – not
necessarily with our own words, but by letting them find the words themselves.

which she recalls how her great-aunt Robbie’s tough love and piano lessons
helped shape the woman she is today:

[8] At home, I continued to work on my own progress as a musician. Sitting at
Robbie’s upright piano, I was quick to pick up the scales and I threw myself into
filling out the sight-reading worksheets she gave me. Because we didn’t have a
piano of our own, I had to do my practicing downstairs on hers. I learned one
song in the piano book and then another. I was probably no better than her
other students, no less fumbling, but I was driven. To me, there was magic in the
learning. I got a buzzy sort of satisfaction from it. For one thing, I’d picked up
on the simple, encouraging correlation between how long I practiced and how
much I achieved. And I sensed something in Robbie as well – too deeply buried
to be an outright pleasure, but still, a pulse of something lighter and happier
coming from her when I made it through a song without messing up. I’d notice
it out of the corner of my eye: Robbie’s lips would unpurse themselves just
slightly.
[9] This, it turns out, was our honeymoon phase. It’s possible that we might
have continued this way, Robbie and I, had I been less curious and more reverent
when it came to her piano method. But the lesson book was thick enough and
my progress on the opening few songs slow enough that I got impatient and
started peeking ahead – and not just a few pages ahead but deep into the book,
checking out the titles of the more advanced songs and beginning, during my
practice sessions, to fiddle around with playing them. When I proudly debuted
one of my late-in-the-book songs for Robbie, she exploded, slapping down my
achievement with a vicious “Good night!” I got chewed out the way I’d heard
her chewing out plenty of students before me. All I’d done was try to learn more
and faster, but for Robbie it was a crime approaching treason. She wasn’t
impressed, not even a little bit.

[10] Nor was I chastened. I was the kind of kid who liked concrete answers to
my questions, who liked to reason things out to some logical if exhausting end. I
was lawyerly and also veered toward dictatorial, as my brother Craig, who often
got ordered out of our shared play area, would attest. When I thought I had a
good idea about something, I didn’t like being told no. Which is how my
great-aunt and I ended up in each other’s faces, both of us hot and unyielding.
[11] "How could you be mad at me for wanting to learn a new song?” “You’re
not ready for it. That’s not how you learn piano.” “But I am ready. I just played
it.” “That’s not how it’s done.” “But why?”
[12] Piano lessons became epic and trying, largely due to my refusal to follow
the prescribed method and Robbie’s refusal to see anything good in my
freewheeling approach to her songbook. We went back and forth, week after
week. I was stubborn and so was she. I had a point of view and she did, too. In
between disputes, I continued to play the piano and she continued to listen,
offering a stream of corrections. I gave her little credit for my improvement as a
player. She gave me little credit for improving. But still, the lessons went on.

[13] Upstairs, my parents and Craig found it all so very funny. They cracked up
at the dinner table as I recounted my battles with Robbie, still seething as I ate
my spaghetti and meatballs. My parents expressed no sympathy for my woes and
none for Robbie’s, either. In general, they weren’t ones to intervene in matters
outside schooling, expecting early on that my brother and I should handle our
own business. They seemed to view their job as mostly to listen and bolster us as
needed inside the four walls of our home. And where another parent might have
scolded a kid for being sassy with an elder as I had been, they also let that be. My
mother had lived with Robbie on-and-off since she was about sixteen, following
every arcane rule the woman laid down, and it’s possible she was secretly amused
to see Robbie’s authority challenged. Looking back on it now, I think my
parents appreciated my feistiness and I’m glad for it. It was a flame inside me
they wanted to keep lit.

In today’s world, it’s easy to hear all that and think that Marian Robinson was

After that, they simply let us be ourselves.
在那之後，他們只是讓我們做自己。

Paragraph 6（第六段）
Reflection（反思）
I see now how important that kind of freedom is for all children, particularly
for girls with flames of their own – flames the world might try to dim.
我現在明白，這種自由對所有孩子來說有多麼重要，尤其是對那些心中自有
火焰的女孩而言——而這些火焰，世界可能會試圖將它們熄滅。
Wider Message（更廣泛的訊息）
It’s up to us, as mothers and mother-figures, to give the girls in our lives the
kind of support that keeps their flame lit and lifts up their voices – not
necessarily with our own words, but by letting them find the words themselves.
身為母親或母親般的人物，我們有責任給予生命中的女孩支持，讓她們心中

而是要讓她們自己找到屬於自己的話語。

Development（發展）
I learned one song in the piano book and then another.
我在鋼琴書中學會了一首歌，然後又學會另一首。
Self-description（自我描寫）
I was probably no better than her other students, no less fumbling, but I was
driven.
我大概並不比她其他學生優秀，也一樣笨拙生疏，但我很有衝勁。
Reflection（反思）
To me, there was magic in the learning.
對我來說，學習之中有一種魔力。
Elaboration（闡述）
I got a buzzy sort of satisfaction from it.
我從中得到一種令人興奮的滿足感。

Realisation（領悟）
For one thing, I’d picked up on the simple, encouraging correlation between
how long I practiced and how much I achieved.
其中一點是，我已經察覺到一種簡單而令人鼓舞的關聯：我練習得越久，取
得的成果就越多。
Observation（觀察）
And I sensed something in Robbie as well – too deeply buried to be an outright
pleasure, but still, a pulse of something lighter and happier coming from her
when I made it through a song without messing up.
我也感覺到 Robbie 身上有某種東西——那份感受藏得太深，還稱不上明顯
的喜悅，但當我順利彈完整首歌而沒有出錯時，她身上仍會透出一絲較輕
盈、較快樂的情緒。
Detail（細節）
I’d notice it out of the corner of my eye: Robbie’s lips would unpurse themselves
just slightly.
我會用眼角餘光留意到：Robbie 原本抿緊的嘴唇會稍稍放鬆一點。
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

Paragraph 9（第九段）
Reflection / Turning Point（反思／轉折點）
This, it turns out, was our honeymoon phase.
後來證明，這只是我們之間的蜜月期。
Hypothetical Reflection（假設性反思）
It’s possible that we might have continued this way, Robbie and I, had I been
less curious and more reverent when it came to her piano method.
如果我面對 Robbie 的鋼琴教學方法時少一點好奇、多一點敬畏，也許我們本
來可以一直這樣相處下去。
Development（發展）
But the lesson book was thick enough and my progress on the opening few
songs slow enough that I got impatient and started peeking ahead – and not
just a few pages ahead but deep into the book, checking out the titles of the
more advanced songs and beginning, during my practice sessions, to fiddle
around with playing them.
但那本練習書夠厚，而我在最初幾首歌上的進度又夠慢，於是我開始不耐煩
，偷偷往後翻看——而且不只是往後翻幾頁，而是翻到書的深處，查看那些較
高階歌曲的曲名，並開始在練習時隨手嘗試彈奏它們。
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

Conflict（衝突）
When I proudly debuted one of my late-in-the-book songs for Robbie, she
exploded, slapping down my achievement with a vicious “Good night!”
當我自豪地在 Robbie 面前首次彈奏其中一首書後段的歌曲時，她爆發了，用
一句嚴厲的「天啊！」狠狠打壓了我的成就感。
Conflict / Reaction（衝突／反應）
I got chewed out the way I’d heard her chewing out plenty of students before
me.
我被她痛罵了一頓，就像我以前聽過她痛罵許多學生一樣。
Self-justification（自我辯解）
All I’d done was try to learn more and faster, but for Robbie it was a crime
approaching treason.
我所做的只不過是想學得更多、更快，但對 Robbie 來說，這簡直是近乎叛國
的大罪。
Conclusion / Reaction（結論／反應）
She wasn’t impressed, not even a little bit.
她一點也沒有被打動，連一點點也沒有。
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

Paragraph 10（第十段）
Contrast / Reaction（對比／反應）
Nor was I chastened.
而我也沒有因此受教或收斂。
Self-description（自我描寫）
I was the kind of kid who liked concrete answers to my questions, who liked to
reason things out to some logical if exhausting end.
我是那種喜歡問題有明確答案的孩子，也喜歡把事情一路推理到某個合乎
邏輯、哪怕令人疲憊的結論為止。
Self-description（自我描寫）
I was lawyerly and also veered toward dictatorial, as my brother Craig, who
often got ordered out of our shared play area, would attest.
我很像律師般愛講道理，同時也有點偏向獨斷；我的哥哥 Craig 可以證明這一
點，因為他常常被我命令離開我們共同的遊戲區。
Elaboration（闡述）
When I thought I had a good idea about something, I didn’t like being told no.
當我覺得自己對某件事有好主意時，我不喜歡被人拒絕。
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

Paragraph 11（第十一段）
Dialogue / Challenge（對話／質問）
"How could you be mad at me for wanting to learn a new song?”
「我只是想學一首新歌，你怎麼可以因此生我的氣？」
Dialogue / Response（對話／回應）
“You’re not ready for it. That’s not how you learn piano.”
「你還沒準備好。學鋼琴不是這樣學的。」
Dialogue / Rebuttal（對話／反駁）
“But I am ready. I just played it.”
「但我已經準備好了。我剛剛不是彈出來了嗎？」
Dialogue / Response（對話／回應）
“That’s not how it’s done.”
「事情不是這樣做的。」
Dialogue / Question（對話／問題）
“But why?”
「但為甚麼？」

Michelle Obama Passage 主線
這篇 passage 是一篇 personal essay 加 memoir excerpt。
前半部分是 Michelle Obama 為 Mother’s Day 寫的個人文章節錄，主要回憶母
親 Marian Robinson 的說話方式和教養方式。後半部分是 Michelle Obama
memoir Becoming 的節錄，透過她小時候跟 great-aunt Robbie 學鋼琴的經歷，具
體展示她的倔強、好奇、好辯，以及父母怎樣保護她心中的 “flame”。
這篇文章的核心可以分成 3條線：
第一條線：
Marian Robinson 的教養智慧在於「少控制，多聆聽」
文章一開始先介紹 Michelle Obama 的母親 Marian Robinson。她是一個說話謹
慎、句子簡短、有智慧、低調又機智的人。她不需要成為眾人焦點，但她令人
喜歡。
這種說話方式直接連到她的 parenting style。
她不急於用自己的聲音壓過孩子。
她更重視讓 Michelle 使用自己的聲音。
這條線告訴讀者：
好母親的力量，不一定來自大量說教，也不一定來自即時控制。
Marian 的力量來自耐心聆聽、給孩子空間、讓孩子練習表達自己。

第二條線：父母的責任是給孩子道德根基，再讓孩子做自己
第5段非常重要，因為它處理一個可能誤解。
有人聽到 Marian 很少說教、很少介入，可能以為她疏忽，讓孩子 rule the roost
。
Michelle 立刻澄清，現實完全不同。
Marian 和 Fraser 其實非常投入。他們給 Michelle 和 Craig 建立了：
● goodness
● honesty
● right and wrong
也就是深厚、持久的 moral foundation。
建立好這個基礎後，他們 simply let us be ourselves。
所以文章的教養觀不是「完全放任」。
它是一種更有層次的教養方式：
先給價值。
再給自由。
過程中保持聆聽和支持。
這條線也連到第6段的 “flame”。
女孩心中的 flame 代表她們的聲音、主見、勇氣、自信、好奇心和生命力。
世界可能會 dim 這些 flame。
母親和 mother-figures 的責任，就是支持女孩，lift up their voices，並讓她們 find
the words themselves。

Question: With reference to paragraph 1, what is the connection between Michelle
Obama’s personal essay and Mother’s Day?
[參照第1段，Michelle Obama 的這篇個人文章與母親節有甚麼關係？]
Answer: The essay shares Michelle’s memories of her mother and is written in
honour of Mother’s Day.
推理：
第1段一開頭已經直接說明：
1. 這是一篇 “in honor of Mother’s Day” 的 personal essay，
2. 而且 Michelle 在文中 shares memories of her mom。
所以「connection」不是單講“這篇文和母親有關”，要同時講兩點：
1. 內容是她對母親的回憶
2. 寫作目的 / 場合是母親節

Mother’s Day 這個關聯。

She would be sweet and witty.

為甚麼「laugh」不是最佳答案？
因為：
第一，題目是問她在社交場合會怎樣反應，最直接可搬去這個情境的是她的
說話方式。
原文最後一句還說：
It’s a style that makes her a favorite of everyone she meets
這句把 meeting people 和她的 style of speaking 直接連起來。
所以「認識新朋友」這個情境，最穩陣的答案是：
她會說話簡潔、審慎。
第二，“smile or a wry laugh” 是附帶，不是固定反應。
注意原文是：
● sometimes
● or
這表示那不是每次都一定出現的行為，只是有時候會配上一個笑容或一聲帶
點幽默的笑。
第三，「laugh」如果單獨寫，太空泛，甚至有點失真。
原文不是說她「一見到人就笑」，而是說她的短句智慧，會「配上一個 smile /
laugh」。
所以如果學生只寫 She would laugh.
這就把一個陪襯細節，錯當成主要反應了。
最穩陣的考場寫法
最安全是：
● She would speak in clipped sentences.
● She would choose her words carefully.

● listened more than lectured = 直接點出 lesson
● nodded patiently = 這個 lesson 的一個例子
那「nodded patiently」到底可不可以？
可以，但最好不要只寫兩個字。
因為如果學生只寫：
nodded patiently
它會比較像一個動作，不夠清楚顯示這是「教養道理」。
如果寫完整些，就更穩陣：
She nodded patiently along to tales of Michelle’s contentious piano lessons.
這樣就看得出：
母親不是急著教訓，而是耐心聽孩子表達。這就連回了 parenting lesson。
學生怎樣知道哪個更好？
考場上可以這樣判斷：
● 如果題目要你找 general lesson / idea / attitude，優先找 較概括的句子
● 如果題目要你找 example / detail，才用較細的動作描寫

listened a lot more than she lectured

兩人都不承認對方的努力。
blank 在 “with neither of them ______” 後面，需要 -ing form。

Question: According to the text, Michelle’s parents “expressed no sympathy” (line
58) for neither Michelle nor Robbie. Give TWO reasons why Michelle’s parents took
the same approach for both Michelle and Robbie.
[根據文章，Michelle 的父母對 Michelle 和 Robbie 都 “expressed no sympathy”。請
寫出兩個原因，解釋他們為甚麼對兩人都採取同樣態度。]
Answer
Any two:
1. They did not want to intervene in matters outside schooling.
【他們不想介入學校以外的事情。】
2. They believed their children should make their own choices / handle their own
business.
【他們相信孩子應該自己作選擇、處理自己的事。】
3. Michelle’s mother may have been happy to see Robbie’s authority being
challenged.
【Michelle 的母親可能暗暗高興看到 Robbie 的權威被挑戰。】
4. They appreciated Michelle’s feistiness.
【他們欣賞 Michelle 的強悍和主見。】
5. They did not mind Michelle being sassy with an elder / Robbie.
【他們不介意 Michelle 對長輩／Robbie 有點大膽頂嘴。】
“- Knowledge pays the highest dividends.” - 知識永遠派發最高的紅利!

但「expected children to handle their own business」可不可以算一點？
這裡要說得很準：
如果它只是當作 “did not intervene” 的重講，風險很高。
但如果學生把它寫成比較獨立的意思，例如：
● They believed their children should solve their own problems / make their
own choices.
仍然不建議把它和 “did not intervene” 配成兩點，因為太近了，容易撞點。
學生在考場上如何知道？
方法：看「是不是同一個理由的延伸」
問自己：
如果我刪去第一點，第二點是不是仍然像一個獨立原因？
如果不是，它多半只是第一點的補充。
這題裡：
● did not intervene
● expected children to handle their own business
第二句其實很像在回答：
為甚麼不 intervene？
答案：因為他們要孩子自己處理。
所以兩句黏得很緊，風險就是被視為同一點。
